description: Source-curated noncancer chronic pain outcomes and receptor biology with distinct evidence lanes; no self-treatment instructions.
editorial_notice: AHRQ's July 2025 final annual systematic review update, a 2021 IASP statement, receptor biology reviews, and a living NIH NCCIH safety summary. These sources have distinct dates and evidence roles.
medical_boundary: Specific studied cannabinoid products may yield small short-term pain improvements but do not establish general efficacy or safety for all cannabis products. Do not replace medical care or change prescribed treatment without a clinician.

sources.title: Living Systematic Review on Cannabis and Other Plant-Based Treatments for Chronic Pain: 2025 Update
sources.authors: Chou R, Ahmed AY, Dana T, et al.
sources.note: AHRQ Comparative Effectiveness Review No. 250, fourth and final annual update; database search through April 28, 2025; noncancer chronic pain with predominantly neuropathic conditions.

sources.title: IASP Position Statement on the Use of Cannabinoids to Treat Pain
sources.authors: International Association for the Study of Pain
sources.note: IASP did not endorse general cannabinoid use for pain because available high-quality clinical evidence was insufficient; historical position, not a 2026 practice guideline.

sources.title: Cannabinoids, the endocannabinoid system and pain: a review of preclinical studies
sources.note: Mechanistic review distinguishing receptor localization, nociceptive physiology, and experimental analgesic pathways from human treatment outcomes.

sources.title: The role of the endocannabinoid system in pain
sources.note: Explains central/peripheral CB1, immune-associated CB2, anandamide, 2-AG and endogenous pain signaling; not a human trial.

sources.title: Cannabis (Marijuana) and Cannabinoids: What You Need To Know
sources.authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH)
sources.note: Clinical risk and regulatory context as consulted Oct 25 2026; living page may be updated.

claims.title: Comparable-ratio THC/CBD oral spray: small short-term benefit
claims.summary: AHRQ 2025 found that certain extracted, comparable THC/CBD-ratio oromucosal sprays probably yield small reductions in chronic pain severity compared with placebo; benefits were concentrated in mostly neuropathic chronic pain studies.
claims.model: Adult noncancer chronic pain; mostly neuropathic; short-term 4 weeks to under 6 months; specific standardized oromucosal preparations
claims.boundary: The benefit belongs to the studied combined formulation, not separately to isolated THC, CBD, whole-plant cannabis, all pain diagnoses, or long-term use.

claims.title: Purified or synthetic THC products: possible small pain improvement
claims.summary: For high-THC-to-CBD synthetic or purified cannabinoid preparations, AHRQ 2025 reported possible small short-term improvements in pain severity, with lower confidence than for comparable-ratio spray.
claims.model: Adults with noncancer chronic pain, mostly neuropathic; studied THC-rich oral products
claims.boundary: Do not generalize the product-level trial findings to every THC product, smoked cannabis, specific doses, or lasting recovery.

claims.title: Oral CBD alone did not improve chronic pain or function in pooled trials
claims.summary: AHRQ 2025 found that studied synthetic or purified oral CBD-only products were not associated with improvements in pain severity or function versus placebo.
claims.model: Adults with chronic noncancer pain; short-term oral CBD randomized studies
claims.boundary: A null pooled result for these studied CBD formulations does not mean CBD is inactive in every biological context; it does not support a general claim that CBD alone relieves chronic pain.

claims.title: Dizziness, sedation and nausea are significant adverse effects
claims.summary: The AHRQ review found increased risk of common adverse effects such as dizziness, sedation and nausea with studied THC-containing and comparable THC/CBD products compared with placebo.
claims.model: Short-term adult chronic-pain clinical trials, product-specific comparisons
claims.boundary: A small mean pain benefit can be offset by harms. Do not infer safety for driving, older adults, combinations with sedatives, or prolonged use.

claims.title: Long-term outcomes and many whole-plant uses remain uncertain
claims.summary: AHRQ 2025 noted insufficient or unavailable evidence for important whole-plant preparations, long-term clinical outcomes, diverse pain conditions, subacute pain, and adolescents.
claims.model: Evidence gaps in the 2025 noncancer chronic/subacute pain review
claims.boundary: No available effect estimate is not proof of safety, effectiveness, or ineffectiveness. Do not promote evidence from standardized formulations to every dispensary product.

claims.title: Opioid reduction or replacement not established by trials in this review
claims.summary: AHRQ 2025 found evidence on changes in opioid use insufficient to draw reliable conclusions for chronic pain treatment.
claims.model: Chronic noncancer pain trials and observational studies evaluated in AHRQ 2025
claims.boundary: This research cannot establish that cannabis should replace prescribed opioids, nor justify abrupt opioid changes.

claims.title: IASP does not endorse general cannabinoid use for pain
claims.summary: The International Association for the Study of Pain concluded in its 2021 statement that high-quality evidence was insufficient to endorse cannabinoids for general pain treatment while acknowledging patients reporting benefit.
claims.boundary: This is a professional evidence position, not a finding that no patient can benefit; evaluate against newer 2025 systematic evidence rather than presenting a single timeless verdict.

claims.title: CB1 receptors modulate presynaptic neurotransmission
claims.summary: CB1 receptors are found at presynaptic sites in central and peripheral neural circuits, including pain pathways. Receptor activation can inhibit neurotransmitter release in experimental contexts.
claims.model: Endocannabinoid neurophysiology and animal/cell models, not clinical efficacy tests
claims.boundary: A CB1 pathway diagram is not evidence that a given cannabis product is a proven pain treatment; THC-associated receptor engagement is not equivalent to an effect size in patients.
mechanism_steps: Gi/o-linked modulation of Ca²⁺ and K⁺ conductances
Reduced neurotransmitter release in relevant model systems
Altered nociceptive signaling, without automatic clinical efficacy

claims.title: CB2-linked immune signaling is studied in inflammatory and neuropathic pain
claims.summary: CB2 is prominent on immune cells; studies explore how CB2 signaling influences neuroimmune and inflammatory processes relevant to pain. Brain expression and model effects are context-dependent.
claims.model: Preclinical neuroimmune systems and experimental pain models
claims.boundary: No human clinical analgesic efficacy follows from CB2 expression or animal nociception findings. This record is not assigned to an individual phytocannabinoid.
mechanism_steps: CB2 on immune and neuroimmune cells
Model-specific changes in inflammatory mediator signaling
Altered experimental nociceptive outcomes in some systems

claims.title: Anandamide and 2-AG are endogenous cannabinoid signals, not phytocannabinoids
claims.summary: The endocannabinoid system includes endogenous lipid messengers anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), their synthesis and breakdown pathways, and cannabinoid receptors.
claims.boundary: These endogenous signals are distinct from the 145 canonical Cannabis phytocannabinoid records; do not create fictitious molecule IDs for them or treat their presence as an analgesic indication.

claims.title: CBD and THC safety must be assessed by product and patient
claims.summary: NIH NCCIH describes cannabis-related impairment, use disorder and psychosis vulnerabilities, plus potential CBD-associated liver effects and clinically relevant drug interactions.
claims.model: General cannabinoid safety and interaction information, not pain-specific comparative efficacy
claims.boundary: Medication review and safety assessment matter. Do not infer a natural product is harmless or substitute general caution for individual medical advice.

claims.title: FDA-approved cannabinoid indications are not chronic pain approvals
claims.summary: NCCIH distinguishes approved cannabinoid medicines for certain epilepsies, chemotherapy-related nausea/vomiting, or HIV-associated appetite loss from the absence of an FDA-approved cannabis-plant chronic-pain indication.
claims.model: US medication/regulatory context summarized by NCCIH
claims.boundary: Specific approved pharmaceutical indications cannot be generalized into approval of cannabis, CBD, THC or whole-plant products as pain therapies.
